clue.text: Writer of 7D is well positioned to secure motor part? Not quite!

indicators.note: Putting letters into position is only a job worth naming if they are not standing in the right one yet.
Securing something means closing on it and holding it fast, so one group of letters shuts around another.
The exclamation says the word just before it stops a fraction short of the mark, so its final letter goes.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters
a motor is a car
an actor's part is a role, docked of its last letter

explanation.surface: Somebody stands in just the right spot to grab hold of a car component, though not quite the right one.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points across the grid: 7 down names the kind of word this writer invented, blending two words into one. 'Motor part' reads as a single phrase and is two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Carroll coined the portmanteau word in Through the Looking-Glass, so he is literally the writer of 7 down's entry.

clue.text: Holiday time in lieu is every so often uncertain? No!

indicators.note: Something done every so often happens at intervals rather than continuously, so the letters are picked up at every second step.
The flat contradiction turns the word before it into its opposite, and it is the opposite whose letters are wanted.

blocks.note: the first, third and fifth letters of these two words
flatly contradicted, 'uncertain' becomes its opposite

explanation.surface: An employee insisting that the time off they are owed for extra hours worked is never in any doubt.
explanation.walkthrough: Time in lieu is hours owed back for overtime, which makes the surface sound like an office grumble; 'every so often' is doing the counting instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Leisure is the free time a holiday is made of — the time itself, not the activities that fill it.

clue.text: Bridge partner devours cake less the icing - most unhealthy

indicators.note: What is devoured ends up inside the devourer, so one word swallows the other whole.
Icing goes on top of a cake, and in a down clue the top is the front, so the leading letter comes off.

blocks.note: the four seats at a bridge table are North, South, East and West, and West partners East
CAKE with the letter on top removed

explanation.surface: A card player at the bridge table wolfing down somebody else's cake once the icing has been scraped off.
explanation.walkthrough: Bridge's four seats are named for compass points, so 'partner' is asking for a direction rather than a person, and the dash stands in for an equals sign.
explanation.definitionFit: The weakest of a group is the one in poorest health, a superlative answering the superlative 'most unhealthy'.

clue.text: Perfume containing iodine first for one qualified in olfactology?

indicators.note: A perfume containing an ingredient holds it within, so the letter is planted inside the other word's letters.

blocks.note: a perfume is a scent
I is iodine's chemical symbol
first written as a numeral keeps these three letters: 1ST

explanation.surface: A perfume laced with iodine, handed to somebody holding a qualification in the study of smell.
explanation.walkthrough: Olfactology is the study of smell, and the question mark admits the definition names only one specialism out of many. 'First' is asking for the tail of 1ST.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone qualified in the study of smell is a scientist — the definition names one branch as an example of the whole class.

clue.text: Ancient overseer refined sugar

indicators.note: Refining puts a substance through a process it comes out of rearranged, and the letters go the same way.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters

explanation.surface: An overseer from long ago is credited with refining the sugar.
explanation.walkthrough: Argus of Greek myth had a hundred eyes and was set to watch over Io, which is why an all-seeing watchman counts as ancient.
explanation.definitionFit: Argus, the hundred-eyed giant posted to guard Io, is the classical byword for a watchful overseer.

clue.text: Upwardly mobile officer overheard hostility

indicators.note: Something overheard reaches you as sound alone, so what you write down need not be spelt the way the speaker meant it.

blocks.note: a ranker is an officer commissioned up from the ordinary ranks, and both words are said the same way

explanation.surface: An officer climbing quickly through the ranks is caught being unpleasant about somebody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upwardly' looks like the reversal instruction a down clue invites, and it is describing a career instead. A ranker is a soldier promoted out of the enlisted ranks.
explanation.definitionFit: Rancour is settled, long-nursed bitterness — hostility of the sort that is felt rather than fought out.

clue.text: Fizzy drink somehow emailed

indicators.note: Leaving the manner of arrival unstated leaves the order of the letters unstated too, so they can be rebuilt.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: A drink that has arrived, by some unexplained route, in your inbox.
explanation.walkthrough: Limeade is the lime version of lemonade. The clue runs to four words, so the one spare adverb has nowhere to hide and has to be the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Limeade is a lime cordial sold carbonated, so 'fizzy drink' names it by its type rather than by a synonym.

clue.text: Cases of fortified wine fellow starts to unceremoniously swill after evening meal

indicators.note: The phrase points at where the following words start, so only the letter each one opens with is taken.
Setting one piece after another puts it behind, so those letters follow what has been built already.

blocks.note: port is the fortified wine of the Douro
a fellow is a man
across much of Britain the evening meal is called tea
the opening letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Crates of port, a bloke, and a thoroughly undignified drinking session once the evening meal is out of the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tea' for the evening meal is everyday British usage rather than the drink. The definition is the luggage sense: a portmanteau is a stiff travelling case hinged to open into two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: A portmanteau is a large travelling case that opens into two equal compartments, so 'cases' is a plain plural synonym.

clue.text: Japanese craft fit with sails, following old comrade to Marseille

indicators.note: A piece described as following another is set down behind it, so these letters take second place.

blocks.note: o is the standard abbreviation for old
to rig a vessel is to fit it out with sails
in Marseille a comrade is an ami

explanation.surface: An old friend down in Marseille is busy fitting a boat out with sails.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Craft' points at boats all the way through the surface — the rigging, the French port — and in the definition it means a practised skill with paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Origami is the Japanese art of folding paper, a craft in the sense of a handed-down skill rather than a vessel.

clue.text: Instructions Ken discovered inside garden ornaments

indicators.note: Read as dis-covered rather than found, it strips the covering off, and a short word's covering is the letter at each end.
The word says the piece is placed within, so the ornaments close around it.

blocks.note: the plaster gnome is the classic British garden ornament
KEN with the letters covering it at either end taken away

explanation.surface: A man called Ken turns up hiding among the gnomes on somebody's lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' is the setter's pun on dis-covered: not found, but having the cover taken off. Garden gnomes are a fixture of British suburban lawns.
explanation.definitionFit: A genome is an organism's complete set of genetic instructions, so the plural covers several such sets of directions.

clue.text: Sewers and streams broadcast - ssssssssssss?

indicators.note: To broadcast is to fling seed wide across a field, which is where these letters end up before you gather them.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
a written-out row of the letter S, and the plural of ess is esses

explanation.surface: Drains and streams giving off one long hiss between them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sewers' wants to be the drains the rest of the surface is about, and it means people who sew. The hiss spelt out is a row of esses, and esses is a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Seamstresses sew for a living, so 'sewers' in its ones-who-sew sense — not the drainage sense — is a plain plural synonym.

clue.text: Go round Scotsman, we hear, bullish sort

indicators.note: The pieces reach us as noise, so what gets written down is a spelling of the sound rather than of the words themselves.

blocks.note: to go round a country is to tour it
Ian is the Scottish form of John and the crossword's usual Scotsman
run together and said aloud, those two pieces come out spelt another way

explanation.surface: You are sent round a Scotsman who is, by all accounts, the bullish type.
explanation.walkthrough: Taureans are born under the bull, which is where 'bullish' comes from — nothing to do with rising markets.
explanation.definitionFit: A Taurean is a person born under Taurus, the bull, so the 'sort' is an astrological label rather than a temperament.

clue.text: Buys Tom a table with hidden leaf sections

indicators.note: Something hidden is present without showing itself, so the letters are sitting unbroken inside the words around them.

blocks.note: seven letters run consecutively across these four words, starting one letter into the first

explanation.surface: Someone buys Tom a table with extra leaves tucked away inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's leaf is a table's fold-out panel; the definition's leaf is the botanical one. Stomata are the pores a plant breathes and sweats through.
explanation.definitionFit: Stomata are the microscopic pores set into a leaf's surface, parts of the leaf itself — 'sections' put loosely.

clue.text: Head off from party, cycling plastered essentially

indicators.note: Cycling sends the letter at one end round to the other while the rest keep their order, the way a bicycle chain comes back round.
The essence of a word is its very middle, so the central letter is the one taken.

blocks.note: a party is a rave, whose R rides round to the back
the central letter of the nine in 'plastered'

explanation.surface: Leaving a party early on a bike, thoroughly drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head off' is the prevent sense, not the departure sense the surface is selling, and 'plastered' is drunk on the surface but only a nine-letter word to be measured in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To avert something is to head it off — to turn it aside before it can arrive — the same prevention sense in both.

clue.text: 1A’s impressive supporters, they bring a lot in

indicators.note: The writer at 1 across gave English the blended word, so the possessive is an instruction to telescope the two words that follow into one.

blocks.note: only the front three letters survive the blend
only the back six letters survive, from the fourth on

explanation.surface: The writer at 1 across has impressive supporters, and they bring plenty in.
explanation.walkthrough: A portmanteau word runs the head of one word into the tail of another, which is the device behind this clue and 15 down as well.
explanation.definitionFit: Importers are the traders who bring goods into a country in bulk, which is what 'they bring a lot in' describes.

clue.text: Means of identifying 1A’s passionless spoilsports

indicators.note: The possessive credits the blend to the writer at 1 across, whose invention it was, and asks for the next two words to be fused into one.

blocks.note: the opening four letters are all that is kept
the last five letters are all that is kept

explanation.surface: Killjoys with no passion left in them, belonging to the writer at 1 across.
explanation.walkthrough: What is left of 'spoilsports' is where ships tie up, so the two surviving halves both mean something on their own before they are joined.
explanation.definitionFit: A passport is the document proving who you are at a border, so the plural is the standard means of identifying travellers.

clue.text: Casual worker behind schedule, a little slow to find pro-forma documents

indicators.note: Asking for a little of a word takes the smallest piece there is, the single letter it opens with.

blocks.note: a temp is a worker taken on for a short spell
running behind schedule is being late
the letter the word starts with

explanation.surface: An agency temp is running late and is a bit slow with the paperwork.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface belongs to one office scene, which is what hides a three-part build. Pro-forma documents are blank layouts kept ready to be filled in.
explanation.definitionFit: A template is a ready-made pattern to work from, which is what a pro-forma document is: a form laid out in advance to be copied.

clue.text: Civilian fighters lost in battle getting one fired

definitions.note: A militia is one body made up of many fighters, so the setter answers a plural definition with a singular collective noun.

indicators.note: Getting something is taking it in, so these letters are received inside the word that gets them.

blocks.note: MIA is the services' shorthand for missing in action
the Roman numeral for one
a fire that has been fired is lit

explanation.surface: Volunteers go missing in a battle and somebody is sacked over it.
explanation.walkthrough: MIA is the military's own shorthand, and 'one fired' looks like a single dismissal while splitting into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A militia is a fighting force raised from ordinary civilians rather than professional soldiers, so it is exactly civilians who fight.

clue.text: Hearing part where water drains when spending penny

indicators.note: Money spent is money gone, so the coin's letter leaves the word rather than joining it.

blocks.note: p is the abbreviation for a penny in British money
a PLUGHOLE hands over that letter from the front

explanation.surface: A remark about where the water goes when you nip off to the loo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spending a penny' is the British euphemism for a trip to the lavatory, which is what makes the surface hang together; the wordplay only wants the coin's letter gone.
explanation.definitionFit: A lughole is British slang for an ear — 'lug' being a dialect word for one — so it is the part you hear with.

clue.text: Afro’s styled up to a point

indicators.note: Hair that has been styled has been worked into a new arrangement, and the letters get the same treatment.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters counting the S

explanation.surface: An Afro styled to a certain height and no further.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is part of the fodder rather than a possessive, which makes it five letters and not four. 'Up to a point' is an idiom meaning partly, and all of it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: So far means to a limited extent and no further, which is precisely what the idiom 'up to a point' says.

clue.text: Banshee pledging to give sanctuary to those easily led

indicators.note: Giving sanctuary is sheltering someone within your own walls, so the letters are being kept inside the words that offer it.

blocks.note: seven consecutive letters straddle the join between these two words

explanation.surface: A wailing banshee promises shelter to the gullible.
explanation.walkthrough: Sheeple is a modern coinage — sheep spliced into people — for a crowd that follows without asking questions.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheeple are people who follow the herd unthinkingly, the blend saying in one word what 'easily led' says in three.

clue.text: Fine fellow from Fontainebleau Bard’s sparring partner?

blocks.note: F is the pencil grade meaning fine
René is a French man's name and Fontainebleau is a French town
Bard is the setter of this puzzle, so what belongs to Bard is his own to call mine

explanation.surface: A fine Frenchman from Fontainebleau, described as the setter's sparring partner.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter signs himself Bard, so 'Bard's' is him saying 'my' — worth remembering whenever a byline turns up inside a clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A frenemy is friend and enemy at once, which is what a sparring partner is: someone you trade blows with in friendship.

clue.text: Put forward member in new deal

indicators.note: The member goes in rather than alongside, so its letters are dropped within the other piece.
Something made new is remade out of the same material, so the letters come back in another order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, four letters
a leg is a limb, a member of the body

explanation.surface: A club member is put up for something under the terms of a fresh agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put forward' means asserted rather than nominated, and it is past tense, which the answer's ending has to match. 'Member' is the anatomical sense: a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: To allege something is to put it forward as a claim without proving it, and both words are past tense assertions.

clue.text: Regularly drop speed (prescribed)

indicators.note: Letters taken at a regular interval means every second one, counted from the start and never varying.

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Someone taking amphetamines at regular intervals, and on doctor's orders at that.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speed' is the drug on the surface and merely a word to count through in the wordplay, while the single bracketed word carries the whole definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To be dosed is to be given a measured amount of medicine, which is what a prescription orders up.

clue.text: Goes around empty palace with King and surveyors

indicators.note: One piece goes around the other, closing on it from both sides at once.
An empty building keeps only its walls, so the word keeps only its outer letters and the middle is cleared out.

blocks.note: to go, in the nursery sense, is to pee
the outside letters of the word with its middle gone
R is Rex, Latin for king, as on the postboxes

explanation.surface: Somebody doing the rounds of a deserted palace in the company of the king.
explanation.walkthrough: Peepers is old slang for the eyes as well as for people who pry, and the palace is emptied of everything except its walls.
explanation.definitionFit: Peepers are those who look others over, so 'surveyors' is the plain ones-who-survey sense rather than the land-measuring profession.

clue.text: Shows model company manuscript

blocks.note: to model for a painter is to sit for them
co is the abbreviation tacked onto a firm's name
ms is the standard abbreviation for a manuscript

explanation.surface: A manuscript from an exemplary firm is put on display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' is wanted as a verb — to model for an artist is to sit — not as the noun the surface offers. Sitcoms are situation comedies, built on one recurring setting.
explanation.definitionFit: Sitcoms are television programmes, so 'Shows' is the everyday broadcasting sense with the plural matching.

clue.text: Charged salesman to lease convertible, ultimately

indicators.note: The ultimate thing is the last one reached, so the word's final letter is what gets taken.

blocks.note: a rep is a sales representative
to lease a property out is to let it
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A salesman is charged with leasing out a convertible when all is said and done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Convertible' is the word most likely to be read as an anagram instruction, and here it is a car whose last letter is wanted. 'Charged' means filled, not accused.
explanation.definitionFit: Replete means filled to capacity, the sense 'charged' carries in a charged battery or a phrase charged with meaning.

clue.text: Shop has rye bread replaced - bit of hair stuck in it

indicators.note: Putting things back in place implies they were lifted out first, and they need not go back where they were.
A bit of a word is a fragment rather than the whole, and the fragment a setter means is the letter it begins with.
The phrase says the stray letter is lodged somewhere among the others rather than tacked on at either end.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters
the letter the word begins with

explanation.surface: A shop where the rye bread has been swapped for something else and a stray hair has got into it.
explanation.walkthrough: Haberdashery is the British shop for buttons, ribbons and sewing sundries; in America the same word sells menswear. The dash carries no instruction and only breaks the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A haberdashery is the shop that sells sewing sundries — buttons, thread, ribbon — so 'Shop' is a plain singular synonym.
